title: Finite-Bandwidth Protection of a Three-Level Quantum Heat Engine Against Parasitic Heat Leaks
authors: Gilberto Aparecido Prataviera, Marcos César de Oliveira
abstract: Finite-bandwidth reservoir engineering can suppress unwanted transitions in a quantum thermal machine, but a physical filter also introduces a finite response time. We study this competition in a continuous three-level heat engine whose hot environment couples parasitically to the cold transition. The corresponding three-state rate network is solved exactly, showing that the parasitic transition produces a hot-to-cold thermodynamic short circuit and yielding a closed threshold for the loss of positive-power operation. We then retain a damped auxiliary mode explicitly as a physical spectral filter. Its Lorentzian response suppresses the detuned parasitic transition, whereas excessive narrowing limits the useful energy throughput. Independent local-GKSL and nonsecular Bloch--Redfield calculations both recover the no-leak Markovian engine in the weak-coupling limit and predict a finite maximum-power bandwidth, although its precise location is model dependent. A frequency-resolved Lorentzian-rate reduction, by contrast, has no interior optimum. The resulting design principle is that spectral selectivity can protect the useful thermodynamic cycle, but a real filter cannot be narrowed without a dynamical throughput cost.
summary: This paper analyzes a three-level quantum heat engine, showing that parasitic heat leaks degrade performance by creating a thermodynamic short circuit. By modeling the system with a physical spectral filter, the authors demonstrate that while spectral selectivity is beneficial, narrowing the filter too much incurs a cost in the engine's achievable power output.
main_problem: The paper investigates how finite-bandwidth reservoir engineering can protect a three-level quantum heat engine from parasitic heat leaks that degrade performance.
main_result: Spectral selectivity can protect the useful thermodynamic cycle, but a real physical filter cannot be narrowed indefinitely without incurring a measurable dynamical throughput cost.
method: The authors compare results from multiple open-system descriptions, including the local GKSL master equation and the nonsecular Bloch–Redfield treatment, to analyze the system dynamics.
model_or_system: The system is a continuous three-level quantum heat engine modeled with useful and parasitic couplings, and the filtering mechanism is introduced via an explicit damped auxiliary harmonic mode.
key_observables: Efficiency ($\eta$), stationary output power ($P$), and the maximum-power bandwidth ($\kappa_\star$).
important_parameters: Filter linewidth ($\kappa$), coupling strengths ($g_h, g_\ell$), and temperature ratios ($T_h/T_c$).
main_assumptions: The analysis compares results from different theoretical approximations (GKSL vs. Redfield) and notes the limitations of the fully secular global model in the weak-coupling limit.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the engine cycle, comparing the useful hot transition against the parasitic coupling, and show the dependence of maximum power on the filter linewidth ($\kappa$).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the ideal rate network, then introduces the physical filter via an auxiliary mode, and finally compares the predictions of the GKSL, Redfield, and rate-only models to derive the final design principle.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of quantum thermal machines by quantifying the unavoidable trade-off between spectral purity (selectivity) and operational speed (throughput) imposed by real-world filters.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Engine cycle and finite-bandwidth protection. (a) The useful hot transition |g⟩↔|e⟩is resonantly coupled to a structured hot filter, while the dashed purple line denotes the unwanted coupling of the same hot filter to the cold transition |i⟩↔|e⟩. The cold bath and the zero-affinity terminal act on the remaining two transitions. (b) Narrow and broad Lorentzian responses centered at ωh, shown at equal resonant height as imposed by 4g2 h/κ = Γh. Narrowing the filter suppresses the detuned response at ωc = ωh −ϵ, while an excessively narrow filter becomes dynamically slow.

Figure 2: Validation of the dynamical descriptions. (a) Recovery of the exact no-leak Markovian engine as the common coupling scale Γ is reduced at χ = 0 and κ = 0.1. The local GKSL and nonsecular Redfield treatments approach P/PM = 1 marked by the blue dashed line, whereas the fully secular global construction does not. (b) Convergence of the maximum-power bandwidth with filter Fock truncation for χ = 1. Both retained explicit filter descriptions converge rapidly, although to different quantitative optima.

Figure 2b shows the independent Fock-space convergence of the two retained explicit filter descriptions. From N = 6 to N = 7, the local-GKSL optimum changes from 13.6332 to 13.6443 in units of Γh, while the Redfield optimum changes from 7.7887 to 7.7938. At the local-GKSL optimum the mean filter occupation is 0.15541 and the highest retained state n = 6 carries only 5.14 × 10−6 probability.
